chapter.title: The dry timber: why Germany wanted to fight again

cards.body: In December 1918 the German army marched home through Berlin with its flags flying. It had just lost a war, yet the fighting had stayed almost entirely outside Germany's borders. On our shared street, the 1919 peace left the German house standing but stripped, with **dry timber stacked against every wall**: a deal that hurt enough to be hated and did too little to disable.
cards.simpler: In December 1918 the German army marched home through Berlin with its flags flying. Germany had just lost the war, but the fighting had stayed almost entirely outside Germany. Think of Germany as a house on a shared street. The 1919 peace deal left the house standing but emptied it out, and left **dry timber stacked against every wall**. The deal hurt enough to be hated, but did too little to stop Germany fighting again.

cards.prompt: You're a Berlin shopkeeper reading the treaty terms in the paper in June 1919. Which headline matches what the deal actually did to Germany?

options.text: Allied troops to occupy all of Germany; country split into four zones
Germany loses land and most of its army, must pay; stays one country
Winners forgive Germany; no land lost, no payments

whyNot.a: That's 1945. In 1919 Allied troops held only the Rhineland strip in the west; the rest of Germany stayed whole and self-governing.
whyNot.c: That's the deal Germans wished they had got, not the one they signed: land, army and money all went.

cards.reteach: Picture the house: still standing, still lived in, but the furniture gone and the owner told it was all his fault. That is 1919. Punished, not dismantled.

cards.title: Hurt, not disabled
cards.body:
The *Treaty of Versailles*, signed in June 1919, was the peace the winners wrote and Germany had to sign. Germany lost about 13% of its land, its army was capped at 100,000 men, and it owed *reparations*, payments for the damage of the war. One clause made it accept the blame for starting it.

Now the twist. You'd think a beaten country would be broken up or occupied. Germany was neither broken up nor fully occupied. Its factories, its 60 million people and its officers stayed in place. So the treaty handed every German **a grievance, and left Germany the muscle to act on it** one day.
cards.simpler: The Treaty of Versailles was the peace deal of June 1919. Germany had to sign what the winners wrote. Germany lost about 13% of its land, its army was capped at 100,000 men, and it owed reparations, payments for war damage. It had to accept blame for the war. Yet Germany was not broken up or fully occupied. Its factories, 60 million people and officers stayed. So Germans got **a grudge, and Germany kept the muscle to act on it**.

cards.title: The flags at the Brandenburg Gate
cards.body: On 10 December 1918, Friedrich Ebert, Germany's new leader, greeted troops returning to Berlin with the words 'no enemy has overcome you.' Crowds threw flowers. The army had in fact been beaten in the field that autumn, which is why it was marching home at all. Six months later the same country signed a treaty saying the war was its fault. Both stories could not be true, and millions of Germans **decided the treaty was the lie**.
cards.simpler: On 10 December 1918, Friedrich Ebert, Germany's new leader, welcomed soldiers home to Berlin. He told them 'no enemy has overcome you.' Crowds threw flowers. In truth the army had been beaten that autumn. That is why it was coming home at all. Six months later Germany signed a treaty saying the war was its fault. Both stories could not be true at once. Millions of Germans **decided the treaty was the lie**.

cards.prompt: Rewind to 1919 and make the peace stricter: Germany is split into five small states, each with a tiny army. Using this chapter's idea, what changes?

options.text: The grievance disappears; nobody resents a treaty they can't fight.
The grievance stays, but the muscle to act on it is gone.
Nothing changes; anger on its own is enough to start a war.

whyNot.a: That mixes up the two halves: harsher terms would make the grievance bigger, not smaller.
whyNot.c: That's the grievance half only: the chapter's point is that 1919 left both the anger and the strength to use it.

cards.reteach: The idea has two parts that must both be true: Germany was made angry, and Germany was left able. Take away the ability and you have an angry neighbour with no matches. Take away the anger and nobody wants a fire.

cards.title: The hot summer
cards.body:
For ten years the timber just sat there. Then in October 1929 the American stock market crashed, American loans to Germany dried up, and by 1932 about 6 million Germans had no job. In photos from those years, men stand on Berlin street corners wearing signs offering to do any work at all. **Hunger turned an old grievance into an urgent one.**

Hitler's Nazi party won 2.6% of the vote in 1928. In July 1932 it won 37%. He promised to tear up Versailles, rebuild the army and take *Lebensraum*, living space, from Poland and Russia. He had already set this out in his book *Mein Kampf* in the mid-1920s. On 30 January 1933 he became chancellor.
cards.simpler: Ten years passed. In October 1929 America's stock market crashed. American loans stopped, and by 1932 about 6 million Germans had no job. Picture men on Berlin street corners wearing signs that said they would do any work at all. **Hunger turned an old grudge into an urgent one.** Hitler's Nazi party won 2.6% of votes in 1928 and 37% in July 1932. He promised to tear up the treaty, rebuild the army and take Lebensraum, living space, from Poland and Russia. He became chancellor, Germany's leader, in January 1933.

cards.body: At a pub quiz, Dev writes 'Versailles caused the war' and sits back, done. But the treaty sat there for ten years and nothing burned; in 1928 the Nazis got fewer than 3 votes in 100. The tell: if an explanation has no room for 1929 and 1933, it has **found the timber and skipped the heat**.
cards.simpler: At a pub quiz, Dev writes 'Versailles caused the war' and sits back, finished. But think about it. The treaty sat there for ten years and nothing caught fire. In 1928 the Nazis got fewer than 3 votes in every 100. A pile of dry wood does not burn on its own. If an explanation has no room for 1929 and 1933, it has **found the timber and skipped the heat**.

cards.prompt: A friend asks for the three-sentence version of why Germany was ready to fight again by 1939. Which one holds up?

options.text: 1919 humiliated Germany but left it whole; 1929 made people desperate; from 1933 Hitler promised to undo the treaty and take land in the east.
1919 occupied and dismantled Germany; Germans rebuilt in secret; Hitler finished the job in 1939.
Germany was never beaten in 1918; it took a rest and picked up where it left off.

whyNot.b: That's the 1945 ending moved to 1919: Germany was punished in 1919, not dismantled, and only the Rhineland strip was occupied.
whyNot.c: That's Ebert's flowers-and-flags version, not what happened: the army was beaten in the field in autumn 1918.

cards.reteach: Three steps, in order: the treaty built the grievance and left the strength; the Depression made the grievance desperate; Hitler offered to act on it. Drop any one and 1939 is much harder to explain.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
The 1919 peace left Germany humiliated but whole, the 1929 crash made the humiliation desperate, and from 1933 Hitler promised to undo the treaty and take land in the east. **Dry timber, a hot summer, and a man who wanted a fire.**

Tomorrow: Britain and France watched Hitler grab land for three years and did nothing. Why?
cards.simpler: Here is the whole chapter in three steps. The 1919 peace deal shamed Germany but left it in one piece. The 1929 crash made that shame desperate, because people were hungry. From 1933 Hitler promised to undo the treaty and take land in the east. **Dry timber, a hot summer, and a man who wanted a fire.** Tomorrow: Britain and France watched Hitler grab land for three years and did nothing. Why?

cards.body: Search for a map of Germany's borders in 1914 next to 1920. Find the strip of Polish land that cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany. Keep that map handy: the story comes back to this strip in 1939.
cards.simpler: Try this now. Search online for a map of Germany's borders in 1914, placed next to one from 1920. Look for the strip of Polish land that **cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany**. It is like a garden path that suddenly has a neighbour's fence running across it. Keep that map handy: the story comes back to this strip in 1939.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in three plain sentences why Germany in 1939 was ready to start a war it had lost so badly in 1918.

dubious_claims: Exercise 1, option a feedback says 'That's 1945' about a Germany 'split into five states', but in 1945 Germany was split into four occupation zones, not five states.

The 'try' card says 'Chapter 2's fire starts right there' about the Polish Corridor, but the teaser says Chapter 2 is about Britain and France letting Hitler grab land; the war over Poland in 1939 comes after that, so the two endings contradict each other.
repairedFrom.why: 'The hot summer' is 119 words, right at the limit, and reads as a list of dates and percentages with no scene to picture; the closing Italy and Japan lines also drift away from the chapter's one question, which is about Germany.
repairedFrom.fix: Cut the last three sentences (Italy/Ethiopia, Japan/China) and use the space for one scene from 1932, such as men queuing outside a Berlin job centre holding signs offering to take any work.
